lead: Every software project does the same work: understand the need, plan, model, build and deliver. Only the amount and order change. The generic process framework gives a common skeleton: five framework activities plus umbrella activities that run across all of them. A team turns the framework into a real process by choosing a task set and a process model.
prereq: You need: 1.2 software engineering practice and principles and 1.3 SDLC phases.

blocks.text: A software process is the set of activities that turns a user need into a delivered product. The generic process framework says every project contains the same five framework activities, whatever its size or style.

items: Communication: agree with the customer and other stakeholders on what to build. Output: a requirement list and scope notes. See Unit 2.
Planning: decide tasks, people, schedule and risks, and write a plan the team can track.
Modeling: build analysis models of what the software must do and design models of how it will do it. See Unit 3.
Construction: write the code and unit test it, so each piece works before it is joined to the rest.
Deployment: install the software, train users, collect feedback and support the release.

blocks.text: The five are a logical order, not a fixed calendar. A team returns to communication when a requirement is unclear, or to modeling after a defect. One full pass is one increment; a large product has many. 1.5 shows how models arrange these passes.
The framework is generic because it is tied to no single model. Waterfall, spiral and agile all contain these five activities; they differ in how often and in what order the activities run.

sections.h3: Tasks, task sets and work products

blocks.text: A framework activity is only a label; the real work is done by tasks inside it. A task set is the tasks a team selects for one project. For every activity it names the tasks, the work products produced, and the quality checks that decide whether a work product is acceptable.

head: Activity
Sample task
Work product
rows: Elicit needs from the operations team
Draw a use case for each actor
Write and unit test one module

blocks.text: The task set is chosen, not copied. A small internal tool with a familiar team needs few tasks and few reviews. A banking or medical system needs more tasks, more work products and heavier checks. Inside one project the task set can shrink for a low-risk increment and grow for a risky one. Choosing tasks by size and risk is the main judgement in process design.

Some work is needed during every activity, so it is called an umbrella activity. Common ones: project tracking and control, risk management, quality assurance, technical reviews, measurement, configuration management and documentation.

items: Tracking and control: compare actual progress, effort and defects with the plan, and correct drift.
Risk management: find risks, rate them, plan responses, review them. See Unit 6.
Quality assurance: set the process and standards, then check the team follows them. See Unit 4.
Technical reviews: walkthroughs and inspections of requirements, design, code and test plans, each held before the work product moves on.
Measurement: collect numbers such as effort per task, defect counts and test pass rate.
Configuration management: identify each work product, control changes, keep approved versions as baselines. See Unit 5.
Documentation: user guides, installation notes and technical notes for the next team.

blocks.text: The name comes from coverage. Configuration management runs in planning when the plan is baselined, in modeling when diagrams are versioned, in construction when branches are created, in deployment when the release is tagged. Quality assurance and measurement also touch every activity.
Umbrella activities are not a sixth phase and are never done once at the end. A project that skips them can still ship code, but it cannot rebuild an old release or prove it was reviewed.

sections.h3: Process patterns, assessment and model families

blocks.text: A process pattern is a named solution to a problem that keeps returning in the process itself. Five fields: name, context (where it applies), problem, solution (process steps to take) and consequences (result and trade-offs). A pattern named "requirements ambiguity" records what to do when a stakeholder cannot state a requirement clearly.

Process assessment checks a team's process against a reference model, grading maturity from ad hoc through managed and defined up to measured and continuously improved. The output is a list of weak areas; process improvement fixes them.

Prescriptive models fix the activities and their order up front; waterfall and incremental are prescriptive. Evolutionary models such as prototyping and spiral let the process grow with the product, covered in 1.5. The concurrent model treats every activity as a simultaneous state: inactive, awaiting changes, under development, under revision or done. Under revision means the work product is being changed after review comments. A design can sit under development while coding starts on the finished parts. Agile details are in 1.6.

figure.caption: The worked example's task counts sit inside each framework activity: 6 + 5 + 8 + 12 + 4 = 35 framework tasks, plus the 3 umbrella tasks, gives 38. Construction's 12 tasks are 12 ÷ 38 = 31.6% of that total; the umbrella tasks cover every activity and are not a sixth step.

spec.title: Task set for one release (worked example)
spec.aria: A downward chain of five blocks — Communication 6 tasks, Planning 5, Modeling 8, Construction 12, Deployment 4 — with an arrow from Deployment back to Communication marked next increment, a separate umbrella block of 3 tasks joined by dashed lines to Communication and Deployment, and Construction marked as 31.6% of the 38-task total.

examples.question: A team defines a task set for one release: communication 6 tasks, planning 5, modeling 8, construction 12, deployment 4. It adds 3 umbrella tasks: a risk review, a quality assurance audit and a configuration baseline. Find the total tasks and construction's share. Also find the share if umbrella tasks are left out.
steps: Umbrella tasks = 3, so the whole task set = 35 + 3 = 38.
Construction share = 12 ÷ 38 = 0.3158..., that is 31.6% to one decimal.
Construction share of framework tasks only = 12 ÷ 35 = 0.3429..., that is 34.3% to one decimal.
The shares differ because umbrella tasks add 3 to the denominator. Umbrella tasks are not a separate phase; they sit across the release.
examples.answer: The task set has 38 tasks (35 framework plus 3 umbrella), and construction holds 31.6% of them, or 34.3% if umbrella tasks are wrongly ignored.
examples.check:
tasks = {"communication": 6, "planning": 5, "modeling": 8, "construction": 12, "deployment": 4}
fw = sum(tasks.values())
umbrella = 3
total = fw + umbrella
print(fw)
print(total)
print(round(tasks["construction"] / total * 100, 1))
print(round(tasks["construction"] / fw * 100, 1))

traps: Counting umbrella activities as a sixth sequential phase. They run across all five framework activities and never finish in one go.
Treating framework activities as SDLC phases. Framework activities are the everyday work inside each increment; SDLC phases describe the whole product life, as in 1.3.
Assuming a task set is fixed. It is chosen per project and can change each increment, by size and risk.
Mixing up process patterns and design patterns. A process pattern is about how work is organised; a design pattern is about software structure, as in Unit 3.
Using the wrong denominator in the construction-share question. The share of the whole task set divides by all tasks, umbrella tasks included.

quiz.q: Name the five framework activities of the generic process framework, in their usual order.
Why are umbrella activities called umbrella activities? Give two examples and say why they are not a phase.
quiz.a: They cover the whole project the way an umbrella covers everything under it, so they run during every framework activity rather than sitting in one place. Examples: configuration management and risk management. They are not a phase because they have no fixed slot; configuration management works on the plan, the models, the code and the release.

quiz.q: A task set lists communication 4, planning 3, modeling 6, construction 9 and deployment 2 tasks, plus 2 umbrella tasks. Find the total tasks and construction's share.
quiz.a: Framework tasks = 4 + 3 + 6 + 9 + 2 = 24. Whole task set = 24 + 2 = 26. Construction share = 9 ÷ 26 = 0.3461..., so 34.6% to one decimal.

quiz.q: A team writes its whole task set as "communication: one task, write the SRS". What goes wrong, and how would you fix it?
quiz.a: One task gives no work products and no quality checks, so nothing can be reviewed and there is no way to know the requirement is complete. It also hides stakeholder identification, elicitation and validation. Fix it by splitting communication into separate tasks, each with a named work product and a check, scaled to the size and risk of the project.

quiz.q: List the five fields of a process pattern and say what each holds.
quiz.a: Name identifies the pattern. Context is where it applies. Problem is the recurring issue. Solution is the process steps to take. Consequences are the result and trade-offs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of process assessment and process improvement?
quiz.a: Assessment compares the team's process against a reference model and finds weak areas, grading maturity from ad hoc upward. Improvement fixes those weak areas, so the process becomes repeatable and measurable.

quiz.q: In the concurrent process model, a design is under development while coding has started on the parts already done. Explain how this is possible and what risk it creates.
quiz.a: Each activity sits in its own state — inactive, awaiting changes, under development, under revision or done — at the same time, so approved design portions move to construction while the rest is still being worked on. The risk is rework: a later revision of a part already coded forces that code to change. Teams control this by baselining a part before coding starts on it.

quiz.q: A small internal tool will be built by two experienced developers in three weeks. How should its task set differ from a banking system's?
quiz.a: The tool needs a small task set with few formal reviews and light documentation, because size and risk are low. The banking system needs more tasks, more work products and heavier checks and reviews, because failure risk is high.

beyond: Not for the exam. Companies audit their process against reference models such as CMMI and the ISO/IEC 12207 life-cycle standard, and keep the task set as a template in an issue tracker so every project starts from the same checklist. Much umbrella work now lives in tooling: configuration management, quality checks and reviews run inside continuous integration pipelines. Process mining reads event logs from these tools to rebuild the process a team actually follows, which is often not the documented one. Search for process mining, software process simulation and ISO/IEC 12207.
